title: Memory types
summary: Agent memory has a short-lived working part (the context window) and long-term parts that persist: episodic (what happened), semantic (what is true) and procedural (how to do things). Name the type before you choose a store.
useIf: An assistant should remember things across turns or sessions, and you must decide what to store, where and how it is read back.
avoidIf: Do not add long-term memory when thread state suffices, or when you cannot meet privacy, deletion or isolation rules for what it stores.

explain.md: The CoALA framework splits agent memory into **working memory** and long-term memory, and divides long-term memory into **procedural**, **semantic** and **episodic** [[r28]]. Working memory is what sits in the context window at the current step. Generative Agents keep a memory stream of natural-language experiences, synthesise reflections from them and retrieve dynamically [[tr16]]. MemGPT borrows the operating-system idea of tiers: virtual context management that moves information between memory tiers, using interrupts for control flow [[r29]].

explain.title: Write path and read path
explain.alt: Conversation events pass through extraction and consolidation into long-term stores for episodic, semantic and procedural memory. At run time, relevant items are retrieved into the working memory in the context window.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  E[Events] --> X[Extract]
  X --> K[Consolidate]
  K --> L[(Long-term memory store)]
  L -->|retrieve| W[Working memory: context window]
  W --> E

explain.md: Managed services follow this shape. Foundry Agent Service memory (preview, checked 2026-10-13) offers three types enabled by default: user profile, retrieved at conversation start; chat summary, retrieved per turn; and procedural memory, retrieved for recurring workflows. It runs phases of extraction, consolidation and retrieval, and is reached through the memory search tool on a prompt agent or the Memory Store APIs [[r13]]. In LangGraph, checkpointers store thread-scoped state, while stores hold cross-thread memory [[r43]]. Claude's memory tool is client-side: Claude asks for file operations under `/memories` and your application executes them [[r41]]. Mem0 is a vendor library whose paper reports gains on the LOCOMO benchmark; the results are vendor-authored [[r40]].

explain.title: Memory is more than a vector store
explain.md: A vector index suits episodic recall. Semantic facts often fit a profile record you can edit and delete, and procedural memory often fits plain text instructions that people can review.

You can name what type of fact each memory is

avoid: Thread state or a profile form already covers the need
You cannot isolate memory per user or tenant
The deployment needs network isolation your memory service does not support

Memory must be human-reviewable: prefer text notes over opaque vectors

pitfalls.symptom: The assistant recalls irrelevant or outdated facts
pitfalls.cause: Everything is stored and retrieved by similarity alone
pitfalls.fix: Consolidate and deduplicate, add recency and scope, and filter by type at retrieval.

pitfalls.symptom: Memory from one user appears for another
pitfalls.cause: A shared store with no scope key on reads
pitfalls.fix: Require a scope such as user or tenant on every read and write, and test isolation.

pitfalls.symptom: The agent repeats mistakes it already learned from
pitfalls.cause: Lessons were never written as procedural memory
pitfalls.fix: Write short, reviewable procedures after failures and load them for matching tasks.

scenarios.title: Personalisation under network isolation
scenarios.situation: An assistant should remember each user's preferences and ongoing projects. The deployment runs inside a private network, and the security team requires that memory data never leave it.
constraints: Per-user memory with deletion on request
unknowns: Does the managed memory service support your network setup?
scenarios.question: Which memory approach fits?

options.name: A store you control inside the network, with scoped profile records and extracted notes
options.why: It satisfies isolation and deletion, and a profile record plus notes covers semantic and episodic needs.
options.tradeoff: You build extraction, consolidation and retrieval yourself.

options.name: Foundry memory in preview
options.why: As of 2026-10-13 it does not support VNet integration, and it is a preview service.
options.tradeoff: A strong fit where network isolation is not required and preview limits are acceptable.

options.name: No long-term memory, only thread state
options.tradeoff: Users must restate preferences each session.

flips.if: The managed service adds the needed network support and leaves preview
flips.then: Reconsider it to avoid building extraction yourself.
A managed or library-based layer saves build time.

scenarios.takeaway: Check isolation support before choosing a managed memory.

scenarios.title: Coding agent that should learn
scenarios.situation: A coding agent keeps asking the same questions about build commands and code conventions in each session. Engineers want the lessons stored where they can read and correct them.
unknowns: How large are the notes after a month?
Which lessons are repository-wide versus personal?
scenarios.question: What do you store, and where?

options.name: Procedural notes as plain text files in the repository that the agent loads at session start and updates after failures
options.why: Procedures are small and reviewable, and files live with the code and can be corrected in review.
options.tradeoff: Notes need pruning, and the agent needs rules for what is worth writing.

options.name: Embed every past chat into a vector index
options.why: Noisy retrieval returns stale or conflicting snippets, and nobody can audit it.
options.tradeoff: Right for recalling specific past episodes by similarity at scale.

options.name: No memory, a longer system prompt
options.tradeoff: Prompt grows by hand, and cannot capture lessons from new failures automatically.

flips.if: Notes become too long to load
flips.then: Split by topic and load only matching files.
Add a shared semantic store with review.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the store to the memory type: procedures like text.

quiz.explain: Working memory is the current context. Episodic memory records past events, semantic memory holds lasting facts and preferences and procedural memory holds how-to knowledge. [[r28]]

quiz.q: Which statement about Foundry Agent Service memory is accurate as of 2026-10-13?
options: It is generally available with VNet support
It is a preview feature with no VNet support and per-store limits
It requires no embedding or chat model deployments
quiz.explain: The docs mark it as preview, list user profile, chat summary and procedural memory, state a VNet limitation and need compatible chat and embedding deployments. [[r13]]

flashcards.back: Procedural, semantic and episodic, alongside working memory [[r28]].

flashcards.front: Foundry memory types, status and one limit?
flashcards.back: Preview as of 2026-10-13: user profile, chat summary and procedural. Limits include 100 scopes per store and no VNet support [[r13]].
A checkpointer saves thread-scoped state. A store holds cross-thread memory [[r43]].
